# Learning Objectives

By the end of today, you should be able to:

1. **Describe** the steps of the k-means algorithm.

2. **Follow** k-means step by step on a small example.

3. **Cluster** Job Scout postings with k-means in R, letting NbClust suggest k.

4. **Explain** the clusters: what is in each one, and what to call it.

5. **Explain** the practical issues (scaling, choosing k) and use k-means in Tableau.

# An Overview of Clustering

???

No time of its own.

---

# The Problem of Clustering

- Given a **set of (high-dimensional) observations**, with a notion of **distance** between observations, **group the observations** into **some number of clusters**, so that:
  +  Members of a cluster are close/similar to each other
  +  Members of different clusters are dissimilar

- **Usually:**
  + The observations are in a high-dimensional space
  + Similarity is defined using a distance measure, e.g.,
      * Euclidean, Cosine, Jaccard, edit distance, etc.

<div class="note" style="font-size:15.5px;"><b class="r">A business example:</b> ChatISA's Job Scout could sort its postings into groups of similar jobs, with no labels to learn from. That is today's question.</div>

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>
**Source:** J. Leskovec, A. Rajaraman, J. Ullman: Mining of Massive Datasets, <http://www.mmds.org>
]

???

Two minutes.

# Clustering in 2D Space: Formulation

- Given a **set of observations (each containing bill length and depth)**, with a notion of **Euclidean distance** between observations, **group the observations** into **3 clusters**, so that:

  +  Members of a cluster are close/similar to each other
  +  Members of different clusters are dissimilar

- Note we are assuming that we did not have a "label/type" for each penguin.

# Comments on the 2D Clustering Problem

Even though the 2D Space clustering problem is the easiest problem to "solve" since we can benefit by plotting the data, **clustering is hard**.

**Some important questions:**

  1. With all the variables being numerical, we often assume **Euclidean distance**. This can be problematic when:
    - variables have significantly different scales
    - we are including information that is not pertinent to grouping

  2. How do you determine the number of clusters (*k*)?

  3. How to represent a cluster of many points?

  4. How do we determine the "nearness" of clusters?

???

Two minutes. Question 1 comes back in the R demo (scaling) and question 2 in the Choose k tab.

# The k-means Algorithm

???

No time of its own.

---

# General Idea

The k-means algorithm clusters data by trying to separate samples in *k* groups of equal variance, minimizing a criterion known as the **inertia** or **within-cluster sum of squares**. This algorithm requires the **number of clusters to be specified**.

<div class="formula">inertia = &Sigma;<sub>records</sub> (distance from the record to its own center)<sup>2</sup></div>

**Inertia is a measure of how internally coherent clusters are; however, it suffers from various drawbacks:**

- Inertia makes the assumption that clusters are convex and isotropic, which is not always the case. It responds poorly to elongated clusters, or manifolds with irregular shapes.

- Inertia is not a normalized metric: we just know that lower values are better and zero is optimal. But in very high-dimensional spaces, Euclidean distances tend to become inflated.

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

**Source:** Clustering, scikit-learn documentation <https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means>
]

???

Two minutes. Lower inertia means tighter groups. Watch it fall in the widget in a minute.

---

# The Steps of the k-means Algorithm

<div class="tiles" style="grid-template-columns:repeat(4, minmax(0,1fr));">
<div class="tile gray"><div class="n">0</div><b>Pick k centers</b><span>The simplest way: choose k records from the data.</span></div>
<div class="tile"><div class="n">1</div><b>Assign</b><span>Each record joins its nearest center.</span></div>
<div class="tile"><div class="n">2</div><b>Move</b><span>Each center moves to the mean of the records that joined it.</span></div>
<div class="tile"><div class="ic">`r fontawesome::fa('rotate')`</div><b>Repeat 1 and 2</b><span>Until the centers stop moving.</span></div>
</div>

<div class="note" style="margin-top:18px; font-size:16px;"><b class="r">No outcome column anywhere.</b> k-means only uses distances: nobody tells it which group a record belongs to.</div>

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

**Source:** Clustering, scikit-learn documentation <https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means>
]

???

Two minutes. Step 0 matters more than it looks: we will try a bad start in the widget.

---

# k-means Step by Step

<div class="km-widget"></div>

???

Eight minutes. Call it, then click: ask for a prediction before every click.

This follows the by-hand handout step for step, with every number the same (centers are kept to 2 decimals, as by hand). Click 0: points 1 and 4 (the two farthest apart) are the starting centers, C1 = (1, 1) and C2 = (5, 7). Round 1 (the first pass): click Assign Next Point once per point, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 (point 4 is skipped). Each click draws the point's distance to both centers on the plot, writes out the square-root formula, puts the point with the nearer center, and moves that center to the mean of its points right away (the dashed arrow). Ask the room which center wins before each click. Point 2: 1.12 vs. 6.10, C1 moves to (1.25, 1.50). Point 3: 3.05 vs. 3.61, C1 moves to (1.83, 2.33). Point 5: 3.15 vs. 2.50, C2 moves to (4.25, 6.00). Point 6: 3.78 vs. 1.03, C2 to (4.33, 5.67). Point 7: 2.74 vs. 1.43, C2 to (4.13, 5.38). Round 2 (the handout's check table): every point is measured against the same two centers. Point 3 switches from C1 to C2 (2.04 vs. 1.78). Use Assign the Rest if the room is ahead of you. Move: C1 = (1.25, 1.50), C2 = (3.90, 5.10), the handout's final answer. Round 3: nothing switches, and Move does not move the centers, so k-means stops. Point at the inertia line: it never goes up. If asked: moving a center after every point is MacQueen's version of k-means; the Steps slide (and scikit-learn) describes the batch version, which assigns every point first. Here both end in the same place.

# Clustering Job Scout Postings in R

```{r jobs_data, include=FALSE}
# Job Scout skills (the Class 25 file): one row per posting and skill.
jobs_file = 'class25_job_skills_2026-11-15.csv'
clusters_file = 'class26_job_clusters_2026-11-15.csv'   # NbClust's clusters, with each posting's title, link and skills
skills = readr::read_csv(file.path('../../data', jobs_file), show_col_types = FALSE)
top30 = skills |> dplyr::count(skill, sort = TRUE) |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 30)
postings = skills |>
  dplyr::filter(skill %in% top30$skill) |>
  dplyr::distinct(posting_id, skill) |>
  dplyr::mutate(has = 1) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = skill, values_from = has, values_fill = 0)
x = postings |> dplyr::select(-posting_id)

# NbClust takes about a minute, so it runs only when the clusters file is missing (delete it to rebuild).
# It needs Job Scout's database (data/chatisa-data/scout.db, kept out of the repo) for the titles and links.
votes_file = '26_nbclust_votes.csv'
if (!file.exists(file.path('../../data', clusters_file)) || !file.exists(votes_file)) {
  set.seed(2026)
  pdf(NULL)
  nb_out = capture.output(
    km_res_nbclust <- NbClust::NbClust(data = x, distance = "euclidean", min.nc = 2, max.nc = 8,
                                       method = "kmeans", index = "all"))
  invisible(dev.off())
  votes = nb_out[grepl("proposed .* as the best number of clusters", nb_out)]
  readr::write_csv(tibble::tibble(line = trimws(sub("^\\*\\s*", "", votes))), votes_file)
  con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), '../../data/chatisa-data/scout.db', flags = RSQLite::SQLITE_RO)
  info = DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT id AS posting_id, title, company, location_city AS city, location_state AS state,
                               category, apply_url FROM scout_postings")
  DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
  skill_list = skills |> dplyr::group_by(posting_id) |> dplyr::summarise(skills = paste(sort(skill), collapse = '; '))
  clusters_out = tibble::tibble(posting_id = postings$posting_id, cluster = km_res_nbclust$Best.partition) |>
    dplyr::left_join(info, by = 'posting_id') |>
    dplyr::left_join(skill_list, by = 'posting_id') |>
    dplyr::arrange(cluster, title)
  readr::write_csv(clusters_out, file.path('../../data', clusters_file))
}
clusters = readr::read_csv(file.path('../../data', clusters_file), show_col_types = FALSE)
votes = readr::read_csv(votes_file, show_col_types = FALSE)$line
stopifnot(nrow(clusters) == nrow(postings), all(!is.na(clusters$apply_url)))
cl_of = clusters$cluster[match(postings$posting_id, clusters$posting_id)]   # cluster of each row of x
k_nb = length(unique(cl_of))
sizes = table(cl_of)
```

Fifteen minutes. This is the Job Scout example promised on Wednesday's Data Mining Models slide, and the answer to today's question. Students copy each tab's code into RStudio and run it; it needs tidyverse, NbClust and factoextra, and every call names its package.

Data: the same file as Wednesday's association rules, one row per posting and skill.

Prep: each posting becomes a row of 0s and 1s over the 30 most common skills. Ask whether we need to rescale: no, every column is already 0 or 1. Contrast with salary in dollars next to years of experience, where salary would decide almost all of the distance.

NbClust Picks k: it takes about a minute on a laptop (69 seconds on mine) and draws two plots while it runs; start it, then talk through the votes on the slide. The majority rule picks k = `r k_nb`, but only `r sum(grepl(paste0('proposed ', k_nb, ' as'), votes))` indices say so. Ask whether that is a landslide. Real data rarely has crisp clusters; the next slide is how we check whether `r k_nb` groups make sense. (If asked: with k = 4, k-means splits the biggest cluster into business and systems analysts on one side and cybersecurity and compliance on the other.)

Viz Clusters: the clusters overlap on the plot because two dimensions cannot show 30. That is why the next slide reads the clusters by their postings and their skills.

---

# Groups of Similar Job Scout Postings

```{r jobs_groups, include=FALSE}
overall = colMeans(x)
centers = sapply(sort(unique(cl_of)), function(j) colMeans(x[cl_of == j, ]))   # skills x clusters: shares
pretty_skill = function(s) gsub('_', ' ', s)
esc = function(s) htmltools::htmlEscape(s)
# the most typical postings in each cluster: the ones closest to its center
d_center = sqrt(rowSums((as.matrix(x) - t(centers)[cl_of, ])^2))
typical = tibble::tibble(posting_id = postings$posting_id, cluster = cl_of, d = d_center) |>
  dplyr::left_join(clusters |> dplyr::select(posting_id, title, company, apply_url), by = 'posting_id') |>
  dplyr::arrange(cluster, d) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cluster, title, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cluster) |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 3) |> dplyr::ungroup()
job_cards = vapply(sort(unique(cl_of)), function(j) {
  gap = centers[, j] - overall[rownames(centers)]
  top = names(sort(gap, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  sk = paste0('<span class="jk-sk">', pretty_skill(top), ' <i>', round(100 * centers[top, j]), '% vs. ',
              round(100 * overall[top]), '%</i></span>', collapse = '')
  tj = typical |> dplyr::filter(cluster == j)
  jobs = paste0('<div class="jk-job"><a href="', esc(tj$apply_url), '" target="_blank"><b>', esc(tj$title), '</b></a> <span>',
                esc(tj$company), '</span></div>', collapse = '')
  paste0('<div class="jk"><div class="jk-h">Cluster ', j, ' <span>', scales::comma(sum(cl_of == j)), ' postings</span></div>',
         '<div class="jk-l">Its most distinctive skills</div><div>', sk, '</div>',
         '<div class="jk-l">Its most typical postings</div>', jobs, '</div>')
}, character(1))
# the skill profile: the 15 skills whose shares differ most across clusters
spread = apply(centers, 1, function(v) max(v) - min(v))
prof = as.data.frame(as.table(centers[names(sort(spread, decreasing = TRUE))[1:15], , drop = FALSE])) |>
  stats::setNames(c('skill', 'cluster', 'share')) |>
  dplyr::mutate(skill = factor(pretty_skill(as.character(skill)), levels = rev(pretty_skill(names(sort(spread, decreasing = TRUE))[1:15]))),
                cluster = paste('Cluster', as.integer(cluster)))
# the table to explore: every posting, with a link to the original job
explore = clusters |>
  dplyr::left_join(tibble::tibble(posting_id = postings$posting_id, d = d_center), by = 'posting_id') |>
  dplyr::arrange(cluster, d) |>   # the most typical postings of each cluster first
  dplyr::mutate(Location = ifelse(is.na(city), state, paste0(city, ', ', state)),
                Job = paste0('<a href="', apply_url, '" target="_blank">', esc(title), '</a>')) |>
  dplyr::select(Cluster = cluster, Job, Company = company, Location, Skills = skills)
```

Expected names: data science and machine learning (python, machine learning), data or BI analyst (dashboards, Power BI, data visualization), and business, systems and security analysts (systems analysis, stakeholder management, cybersecurity, compliance). # Summary of Practical Issues

- Rescale numeric data prior to k-means implementation. The scaling can be:
  + a z-transformation (subtract the column's mean, divide by its standard deviation)
  + a 0-1 scaling
  + converting count data into percentage or counts per a certain number of the population
  + etc.
  + (Job Scout's 0/1 skill columns are already on one scale.)

- Use more than one metric to determine k when using k-means clustering

- Your cluster solution is not the end result, you will need to:
  + visualize it in appropriate way (as in the Viz Clusters tab and the Skill Profiles heatmap, [spatially](https://fmegahed.github.io/covid_analysis_final.html#33_Visualizing_the_Clustering_Results), over time, etc.)
  + Attempt to explain the cluster membership using an appropriate binomial/multinomial model (e.g., see [this analysis](https://fmegahed.github.io/covid_analysis_final.html#4_Explanatory_Modeling_of_Cluster_Assignments))

???

# Summary of Main Points

- Describe the steps of the k-means algorithm: pick k centers, assign each record to its nearest center, move each center to the mean of its group, and repeat until the centers stop moving

- Follow k-means step by step: inertia (the within-cluster sum of squares) never goes up from one step to the next; a bad start can end in a worse answer

- Explain the practical issues: rescale first, use more than one measure to choose k, then visualize and explain the clusters

- Cluster Job Scout postings in R (`NbClust::NbClust()` to suggest k, `stats::kmeans()`, `factoextra::fviz_cluster()`), then explain the clusters by their skills and their jobs

- Use k-means in Tableau (Analytics pane &gt; Cluster)
